title: Are we in a simulation?
dek: Twelve on a hand. Seventy-two years to one degree of sky. 432 squared sitting beside the speed of light. The same numbers, and two ways to read them.
socialHook: 72 years for one degree of sky. 25,920 for the full turn. 432 squared sits next to the speed of light. Are we in a simulation, or counting a clock we built?
socialTitle: Are we in a simulation? The numbers won't say.
heroAlt: The Earth, fully lit, photographed by the Apollo 17 crew on the way to the Moon in December 1972.

marginNote.label: Both doors stay open.
marginNote.body: A repeated number can be a tool we kept. It can also be a mark someone left. This piece does not pick.

blocks.text: Are we in a simulation?
Not as a joke, and not as a verdict. As a question you can actually hold still for a few minutes.

If a world were built, you might expect the builder to leave a grammar. Ratios. Counts. A few numbers that keep meeting each other in the sky, in the body, and in the old stories. People have been collecting those meetings for a long time. The usual ones are 12, 60, 72, 360, 432, and 25,920.
The hand that counts to sixty
Ancient Mesopotamian mathematics used base 60, not base 10. Sixty divides cleanly by 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 12, 15, 20, and 30. Handy for fractions, for trade, for land, and for the sky.
We still live inside it. Sixty seconds. Sixty minutes. A circle of 360 degrees.

One old way of arriving at 60 is still on your hand. The thumb of one hand can touch twelve finger-bones, three on each of the other four fingers. The other hand counts the rounds, up to five. Twelve times five is 60.

blocks.alt: A photograph of a hand counting to twelve by touching the finger-bones with the thumb.
blocks.caption: Counting to twelve on the bones of one hand. Photo: Rhetos, Mathe-AC Lernwerkstatt, Aachen, 2021. CC0.

blocks.text: A useful count can just be a tool that worked, so people kept it. It can also be a strange thing to find still running the clock, the compass, and the circle, thousands of years later. Both of those sentences can be true at once.
A degree every 72 years
Earth spins once a day and goes around the Sun once a year. It also wobbles, slowly, like a top. The direction of that axis drifts. Astronomers call it the precession of the equinoxes.

A round number used for the full cycle is 25,920 years. Divide that by 360 degrees and you get 72. One degree of sky about every 72 years. Divide 25,920 by 12, 24, 36, 48, and 60 and you get 2,160, 1,080, 720, 540, and 432.

blocks.alt: A 1902 printed diagram of the precession of the equinoxes, showing the slow wobble of Earth's axis.
blocks.caption: Precession of the equinoxes, from Simon Newcomb, Astronomy for Everybody, 1902. Public domain.

blocks.text: Then 432 shows up again, in a different costume. A day has 86,400 seconds. The Sun’s diameter is often given as about 864,000 miles. The Moon’s diameter is about 2,160 miles, the same number as 25,920 divided by 12. And 432 squared is 186,624, close to the speed of light in miles per second.

Miles and seconds are units we chose. Change the unit and some of those neighbours move apart. That belongs in the picture. So does the other fact: 12, 60, 72, 360, and 25,920 meet each other before anyone picks miles. A hand. A clock. A circle. A slow turn of the sky.
The cone, the tone, the old stories

Sumer arrives in this story as a sudden pile of writing, wheels, boats, looms, ploughs, and organised maths. The Sumerian King List speaks of kingship lowered from heaven. Stone figures carry a small bucket and a cone.

One reading is that the stories remember teachers, and that the knowledge was handed over rather than only invented. Another reading is that cities often explained power by saying it came from above. The texts support the wonder. They do not force you to stop wondering.

The pine cone sits in the same conversation. Seed scales often pack in counts that follow the Fibonacci sequence. The pineal gland, deep in the brain, has struck people for centuries as a small echo of that cone. From there the thought grows: maybe the gland is a receiver, and maybe a tone is one of the signals.

blocks.alt: A pine cone photographed from above, its scales spiralling out from the centre.
blocks.caption: A pine cone from above. Photo: Richard Flink, 2008. CC BY-SA 2.0.

blocks.text: The tones people name are 144, 288, 360, and 432. Sound can organise matter. A plate of sand, set vibrating, draws a standing-wave figure. That is cymatics, and it is ordinary physics. Whether 432 Hz is a preferred tone of the world, or one tone among many that can draw a figure, is a question the plate leaves in your hands.

blocks.alt: A square metal plate with sand gathered into a symmetrical standing-wave pattern.
blocks.caption: Sand on a vibrating Chladni plate. Photo: High Contrast, 2011. CC BY 3.0 DE.

blocks.text: Two ways to hold it

Way one: a built world would look a bit like this. A few ratios, reused. A clock that still matches the sky. A body that rhymes with a plant. Stories that say the knowledge came down. You would not get a signed letter. You would get a grammar.

Way two: we are pattern-making animals, and we are good at it. The same gift that found the seasons can also stitch a hand, a hymn, and a mile into one sentence. Some of the stitches depend on units we invented. Some do not.

I can stand in either room without throwing the other one out. The counts are real. The wobble of the axis is real. The plate really draws. What the repetition means is still a choice you get to keep making.
The numbers are really there. What they are doing is still open.
If the same counts can be a clock we kept and a note someone left, what would you need to see before you knew which one you were looking at?
